## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
```
:::


## The question

Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate
drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a
margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.

Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won't.

**In this analysis, I look at total commuters across counties in
Connecticut, and ask which communities we measure most and least
reliably. As Connecticut features a large commuter region to New York in
the southwestern part of the state, I am curious about the general
patterns across Connecticut and where census estimates tend to be more
reliable.**

## Choosing what to measure


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_state <- "CT"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B08303_001"     # the variable code, in quotes
```
:::


## Pulling the data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
```
:::


Let's look at what came back.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(county_data)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9 5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
head(county_data)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  <chr> <chr>                                            <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>
```

**My data has 9 rows, matching the 9 census-used planning regions in the

## How big is the margin of error?

A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an
estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across
places, we need it as a percentage.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)
```
:::


Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 9 × 4
  NAME                                                    estimate   moe moe_pct
  <chr>                                                      <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region, Connecticut      42707  1095   2.56 
2 Northwest Hills Planning Region, Connecticut               49420  1043   2.11 
3 Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Region, Connec…    78097  1309   1.68 
4 Greater Bridgeport Planning Region, Connecticut           136932  2110   1.54 
5 Southeastern Connecticut Planning Region, Connecticut     122762  1814   1.48 
6 Western Connecticut Planning Region, Connecticut          256479  3731   1.45 
7 Naugatuck Valley Planning Region, Connecticut             198589  2586   1.30 
8 South Central Connecticut Planning Region, Connecticut    245723  2876   1.17 
9 Capitol Planning Region, Connecticut                      411729  3849   0.935
```


:::
:::


**The Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region has the largest `moe_pct`
relative to its estimate, measuring at about 2.6%.**

## Sorting counties into reliability categories


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 2 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence     1
2 Low confidence      2
3 Moderate            6
```


:::
:::


As the percent margin of error for all 9 planning regions of Connecticut
fell well into the original \<5% cutoff for `High confidence`, the
categories were adjusted so that `High confidence` represents a margin
of error of \<1%, `Moderate` represents a margin of error of \<2%, and
`Low confidence` represents a margin of error of \>2%.

## Is the margin of error bigger in small places?

To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the
same row. That means a **wide** pull.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                                          myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                                          <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 09110 Capitol Planning Region, Connecticut          411729   3849 969029    NA
2 09120 Greater Bridgeport Planning Region, Connecti… 136932   2110 326296    NA
3 09130 Lower Connecticut River Valley Planning Regi…  78097   1309 174983    NA
4 09140 Naugatuck Valley Planning Region, Connecticut 198589   2586 452303    NA
5 09150 Northeastern Connecticut Planning Region, Co…  42707   1095  95829    NA
6 09160 Northwest Hills Planning Region, Connecticut   49420   1043 112848    NA
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 1  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 2 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))
```
:::


Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability
category.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_population))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          1        969029 
2 Moderate                 6        403440.
3 Low confidence           2        104338.
```


:::
:::


**The `avg_population` of high-confidence planning regions are much
higher than the `avg_population` of low-confidence planning regions, the
former being about 969,029 and the latter being about 104,338.**

## What this means for policy

Through this exercise, we learned that we know the least about the
Northeastern Connecticut and the Northeast Hills planning regions. As
both of these planning regions feature the lowest populations in the
state, they feature the lowest sample sizes and largest percent margin
of error (\>2%) in the American Community Survey data set.

It is important to understand the variability of reliability within the
ACS data set when making policy decisions, as certain planning regions
with lower sample sizes may be underrepresented. For example,
communities in the northeastern and northwestern corners of the state
may appear to have fewer commuters than in the Hartford region, though
in reality it may be an artifact of sample size. Poor data literacy in
the policy making process could result in a reduction in bus service
within these regions, despite them in reality having a larger need for
public transportation than anticipated.

## Plotting Data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(sf)
planning_regions <- read_sf('assignments/data/CT_Planning_Regions.geojson')

planning_regions <- left_join(planning_regions, county_wide, by=c('PlanningRegionFIPS_GEOID'='GEOID'))

planning_regions<- planning_regions %>%
  arrange(match(reliability, c("High confidence", "Moderate", "Low confidence")))
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(patchwork)
reliability_map <- ggplot(planning_regions) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill=reliability), color='white') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("High confidence" = "#b71c1c", 
                               "Moderate" = "#f4977a", 
                               "Low confidence" = "#fce4de"),
                    breaks = c("High confidence", "Moderate", "Low confidence")) + 
  labs(title='Reliability of Census Estimates', fill=NULL) +
  theme_void()

pop_map <- ggplot(planning_regions) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = popE), color = 'white') +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1) +
  labs(title='Population', fill=NULL) + 
  theme_void()

reliability_map + pop_map
```
